lessons.title: Making an appointment
lessons.goal: Make, confirm and cancel an appointment on the phone.

tip.title: Allô and polite questions
tip.body: Allô (a-LO) is only used on the phone. Prendre rendez-vous = to make an appointment; in rendez-vous the z and the s are silent: ran-dé-VOU. Vous pourriez … ? (could you …?) sounds softer than Vous pouvez … ?. Say who you are with C'est … à l'appareil (… speaking). Times: neuf heures et demie, or neuf heures trente in schedules. End the call with Au revoir, bonne journée !

lessons.title: Problems and complaints
lessons.goal: Report a problem, complain politely and ask for a solution.

tip.title: depuis + present tense
tip.body: To say how long a problem has lasted, French uses the present tense with depuis: Le chauffage ne marche plus depuis lundi (hasn't worked since Monday), J'attends depuis une heure (I've been waiting for an hour). Don't use the passé composé here. Ne … plus means 'no longer'. Start a complaint calmly with J'appelle parce que … and ask with Je voudrais … . In chauffage, au sounds like 'oh': cho-FAJ.

lessons.title: Who's calling?
lessons.goal: Ask for someone, leave a message and give your number.

tip.title: C'est de la part de qui ?
tip.body: Key phone phrases: C'est de la part de qui ? (Who's calling?), Ne quittez pas (Hold the line — literally 'don't leave'), Je vous la passe (I'll put you through to her; le for him). Phone numbers are said in pairs: zéro six, douze, trente-quatre… To spell your name, learn the tricky letters: e sounds like 'uh', i like 'ee', g like 'zhay' and j like 'zhee'.

lessons.title: le, la, les — lui, leur
lessons.goal: Replace people with direct and indirect object pronouns.

tip.title: Direct and indirect object pronouns
tip.body: Direct object (no à): le, la, l', les — Je rappelle Marc → Je le rappelle. Indirect object (à + person): lui (to him or her), leur (to them) — Je téléphone à Marc → Je lui téléphone. Trap for English speakers: appeler takes a direct object (je l'appelle) but téléphoner à takes an indirect one (je lui téléphone); dire à, parler à, écrire à and envoyer à also use lui/leur. The pronoun goes before the verb (Je ne lui téléphone pas), or before the infinitive: Je vais le rappeler. Me, te, nous, vous work for both.

culture.title: Allô ? Phones across the francophonie
culture.body: In France people usually answer with Allô ? or Allô, oui ?, and businesses give their name plus bonjour. It's polite to say who you are straight away: Bonjour, c'est Alex Martin. A mobile phone is un portable in France, un GSM in Belgium and un cellulaire (or un cell) in Québec; in Switzerland you may still hear the older word natel, though portable is common. A text is un texto or un SMS. Numbers are read in pairs: zéro six, douze, trente-quatre…

tip.body: You've talked about your weekend, travel, health, home, work, plans, clothes and phone calls. Speak in full sentences, take a breath before you answer, and don't worry about small mistakes — being understood is what counts. Bon courage !
